newsitem.title: BRAZIL: AIDS threat sharpens for Brazilian children.
newsitem.headline: AIDS threat sharpens for Brazilian children.

text.p: An estimated 183,000 Brazilian children are at risk of losing their mothers to the AIDS virus, leaving many of them homeless and destitute, according to a survey published on Tuesday.

It estimates that 10,600 Brazilian children under 14 years of age have already lost their mothers to AIDS, 34,600 have mothers with AIDS and 137,800 have mothers infected with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS. Of these 183,000 children, eight percent are HIV-infected themselves.

"It's like saying 183,000 children have boarded an airplane without pilot, co-pilot or flight attendants, flying without direction, lost in the air," said Miguel Fontes, one of the authors of the survey. "We want these children to disembark again as citizens and members of the workforce."
The survey backed by UNICEF was carried out by the John Snow institute, a U.S.-based non-governmental organisation for social development which administers the Global Orphan Project.
Fontes said preventive measures were necessary to slow the rate at which children were losing their parents and to contain the "unsustainable" costs involved in providing for these children.

The survey estimates the number of 10,600 children orphaned by AIDS could more than double by the year 2000 and the upkeep for each orphan could cost up to $16,000 annually. On the other hand, preventive measures would only cost between $400 and $1,000 annually per child, Fontes added.

He said preventive measures should include better access to HIV testing and AIDS medication, programmes directed at low income families, custody plans for orphans and legal measures supporting families affected by AIDS.

Brazil has the third-highest incidence of AIDS in the world with an estimated 425,000 people infected with HIV, according to figures from UNAIDS, the United Nations AIDS programme. But estimates by the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) run as high as 860,000.

Brazilian Health Ministry figures show AIDS is spreading faster among women than among men, heterosexual transmission of the virus is increasing and unlike before, the illness now mainly affects the lower income urban population.
"It (AIDS) is no longer an illness of (so-called) high-risk groups," Fontes said.
